verdict.root_cause: checkoutservice keeps accepting traffic and logging PlaceOrder entry lines throughout the degraded period, but from ~13:34 onward those requests emit no terminal line at all — no payment, email or message-write follow-on — whereas complete success sequences appear earlier (last at 13:07:19) [tr_5d8601d884d2]. Error ratio moved from a flat-zero baseline (413 samples, sd 0) to a mean of ~0.217 with peaks near 0.667, first crossing at 13:10:15 and escalating at 13:34 [tr_e37bcc2d8bf3]. The stall sits before the payment hop: paymentservice pairs every Charge with a sub-millisecond completion, all info severity, one stable replica, no declines or restarts [tr_db26d6344f2d]. No deploy, config edit or flag flip is on record for either service in the queried span [tr_c3095b72b399][tr_f37326243c8e]. Requests accepted, work begun, nothing returned, partial rather than total failure — that is checkoutservice blocking on a slow dependency in the pre-payment path (cart, currency, or shipping quote), consistent with those services alerting within 90s. The specific hop is unidentified: the trace query that would attribute the wait failed with a backend 500 [tr_77ccced59d8c].
verdict.reasoning: The mechanism is read from log shape, not error text: entry lines with no terminal line of any kind is the signature of waiting on a call that never returns, not of a service producing wrong answers [tr_5d8601d884d2]. Metrics confirm a genuine state change from a zero baseline and a partial failure (max 0.667), ruling out crash-loop or hard-down [tr_e37bcc2d8bf3]; logs independently rule out OOM/restart and ingress outage. Payment is exonerated as the slow hop by sub-millisecond request-to-completion pairs [tr_db26d6344f2d]. Not bad_deploy or bad_config: no change record exists in what was queried, and a change would in any case be the act, not the mechanism — the failure is the wait. Not resource_exhaustion: nothing shows checkoutservice running out of anything, though no saturation metric was ever collected. remediation_class is 'none' because no target is identified — there is nothing to revert, and restarting or scaling checkoutservice would not fix a stall originating in an unnamed dependency.
open_questions: Which dependency is checkoutservice blocking on? The pre-payment path (cartservice, currencyservice, shippingservice/quoteservice) was never queried and traces failed with a 500 [tr_77ccced59d8c]. Retry traces before acting.

All change queries covered 13:36 Sep 1 -> 13:38 Sep 2, i.e. after onset, not before — the specialists flagged this themselves [tr_c3095b72b399][tr_f37326243c8e]. A change shortly before 13:10 remains entirely possible and would alter remediation.

Is intra-checkoutservice saturation (connection pool, threads, memory) the real mechanism? Only error ratio was evaluated; a saturated outbound pool would produce this same log shape and would point to a different fix.

proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no change in system behaviour should be observed. What should happen instead is investigative: re-run the checkoutservice trace query that returned HTTP 500 [tr_77ccced59d8c] and query the pre-payment dependencies (cartservice, currencyservice, shippingservice, quoteservice) for latency percentiles and error ratio, plus checkoutservice saturation metrics (outbound connection pool, goroutine/thread count, memory). Those queries either name a stalling hop — a p99 that rose at or before 13:10:15 and stepped again at 13:34 — or they show checkoutservice itself saturated with healthy dependencies. Also re-run change_history with a window that actually precedes 13:10, since both change queries covered 13:36 onward only [tr_c3095b72b399][tr_f37326243c8e] and therefore rule out nothing before onset.
proposal.if_wrong: Abstention is wrong if the incident is in fact simple process state on checkoutservice that a recreate would clear — but nothing in the evidence supports that: the log stream shows a live process emitting PlaceOrder entry lines continuously with no restart banner and no error severity at all [tr_5d8601d884d2], which is the shape of blocking on a dependency, not of a wedged process. It is also wrong if orders self-recover before the follow-up queries land, in which case the window closes and the stalling hop becomes unattributable. Concretely: if the retried trace query names a child span carrying the wait, or if a pre-13:10 change record surfaces, a targeted proposal becomes possible and this abstention is superseded.
proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is continued customer-visible loss: PlaceOrder requests keep arriving and keep producing no payment, email or message-write line, so orders are silently dropped for as long as this persists, and error ratio stays near its 0.667 peak. The risk of the alternative — restarting checkoutservice on this evidence — is higher: it would discard every in-flight PlaceOrder, would not touch a slow dependency if that is the mechanism, would destroy the log and connection state needed to identify the hop, and is explicitly not reversible. rollback_image and revert_config fail their preconditions outright: no deploy, image change, or config edit is on record for checkoutservice or paymentservice, and the queried windows never covered the period before onset, so there is no prior tag or prior config to restore. scale_service is unavailable in this world.
proposal.blast_radius: No change, so no one sees anything new. For contrast, had an action been taken on checkoutservice, its inbound callers — frontend, and through it loadgenerator — would see connection resets during the recreate, and its downstreams in the pre-payment path (cartservice, currencyservice, shippingservice, quoteservice) plus paymentservice, emailservice and the accounting/fraud consumers of the order message would see traffic drop and then resume. The existing degradation already reaches all of these: every listed seed service alerted.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Ten services alerting within ninety seconds starting at checkoutservice and frontend is a broad, critical failure that cannot be dismissed, and no open incident could account for it. The fan-out pattern fits either a checkout-path dependency failure or a deploy, so the fault class is genuinely open at this stage.
